instruction: Why are some months longer than others?

The ancient Romans based their calendar on the Moon's phases, but because the Moon takes about 29.5 days to orbit Earth, keeping a twelve-month calendar aligned with Earth's 365.25-day trip around the Sun required some adjustments. Julius Caesar and later Emperor Augustus added days to different months to make the math work out. February ended up with the leftover days, which is why it is the shortest, while the others got 30 or 31 days to make sure the whole year matches the solar cycle.

Later, in 1582, Pope Gregory XIII refined it into the calendar we use today, keeping January 1st as the official start of the new year to mark a fresh beginning.

By moving New Year's Day to January 1st, we made sure that the new year started on January 1st every year, which is how we celebrate it today!
